name: Belgium

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally
paths.note: Dividends bear the 30% final withholding (on the amount net of any foreign withholding); gains realised on financial assets bear the new 10% tax (Law of 6 April 2026, from 1 January 2026); securities accounts above EUR 1 million pay 0.30% a year (Programme Law of 30 May 2026). Inheritance tax is the Flemish one (3% / 9% / 27% per heir) on the portfolio and the home; unrealised gains are not taxed at death.

paths.name: Family investment company (BV/SRL)
paths.note: A Belgian BV owned by the parents holds the portfolio. It pays 25% corporate tax on portfolio dividends (net of foreign withholding, no credit) and on gains (no participation exemption below 10% or EUR 2.5 million), the same 0.30% securities-account tax and a running cost; payouts bear the 30% dividend withholding. The shares are in the estate at market value, so Flemish inheritance tax applies to them as to the portfolio. A foreign foundation or trust is not modelled because the Cayman tax (art. 5/1 CIR 92) taxes the founder on its income as if received directly, and a Belgian private foundation is not modelled (see the open questions).

checks.working: Top marginal rates; the real family has about EUR 600,000 of dividends a year, so the small allowances are ignored. Belgian-source dividends 20,000 at the 30% withholding (art. 269 section 1, 1 CIR 92) = 6,000; the EUR 859 dividend exemption is ignored. Gains 15,000 at 10% (new art. 90 al. 1, 9, c CIR 92; rate in art. 269 section 1, 5 and Circular 2026/C/74 points 118-119) = 1,500; the annual exemption of EUR 10,000 (art. 96/2, 2: EUR 4,855 indexed) is ignored because the real family realises about EUR 450,000. Securities-account tax: the portfolio of 10,000,000 is above the EUR 1 million threshold, so the whole value bears 0.30% (Programme Law of 30 May 2026) = 30,000; the 10% cap applies only up to EUR 1,030,927.84. Total 6,000 + 1,500 + 30,000 = 37,500.

Foreign dividends 20,000 with 15% withholding at source = 3,000. Belgium taxes the amount net of the foreign tax (administrative commentary on art. 22 CIR 92 and Circular 2020/C/96): 17,000 at 30% = 5,100; the foreign tax is not credited. Gains 15,000 at 10% = 1,500 (new art. 90 al. 1, 9, c CIR 92; exemption ignored as above). Securities-account tax 0.30% x 10,000,000 = 30,000. Total 5,100 + 1,500 + 30,000 = 36,600.

Belgian company paying the 25% corporate tax rate (art. 215 CIR 92; the 20% SME rate on the first EUR 100,000 is ignored, the real profit is about EUR 1 million). Portfolio dividends below 10% and EUR 2.5 million get no dividends-received deduction: 20,000 x 25% = 5,000. Gains on such shares are not exempt (art. 192 CIR 92 follows the same participation conditions): 15,000 x 25% = 3,750. Securities-account tax on the company's account 0.30% x 10,000,000 = 30,000 (companies are liable; assumed not deductible). Running cost of the BV: accountant at the upper end of the EUR 2,500-4,500 a year quoted for a BV = 4,500. Total 5,000 + 3,750 + 30,000 + 4,500 = 43,250. The 30% payout withholding is excluded. Running costs are deductible from the BV's taxable profit (art. 49 CIR 92): 25% x (35,000 - 4,500) = 7,625 + 4,500 + 30,000 = 42,125.

Foreign dividends 20,000 with 15% withholding = 3,000. The company's taxable dividend is the amount net of the foreign withholding, 17,000, at 25% = 4,250; generally no foreign tax credit is available for foreign dividends (PwC). Gains 15,000 x 25% = 3,750. Securities-account tax 30,000. Running cost 4,500. Total 4,250 + 3,750 + 30,000 + 4,500 = 42,500. Running costs are deductible (art. 49 CIR 92): 25% x (17,000 + 15,000 - 4,500) = 6,875 + 4,500 + 30,000 = 41,375.

Flemish inheritance tax, direct line (Flemish Tax Authority tariff), calculated per heir with no allowance for an adult child. Each child receives 10,000,000 / 3 = 3,333,333.33, all movable (listed securities), so one scale applies: 3% of the first 50,000 = 1,500; 9% of the next 200,000 = 18,000; 27% of the remaining 3,083,333.33 = 832,500. Per child 852,000; three children 2,556,000.

The BV shares are movable assets valued at market value, about the portfolio, with no business relief for a portfolio company: same Flemish calculation as for personal holding. Each child 3,333,333.33: 1,500 + 18,000 + 27% x 3,083,333.33 (= 832,500) = 852,000; three children 2,556,000.

assumptions: The national file represents Flanders for inheritance tax (3% / 9% / 27%). Brussels-Capital and Wallonia have other scales and are not modelled, although the family's likely home (Uccle, Ixelles) is in Brussels.

The family has just arrived: the capital gains tax values assets at the first day of Belgian tax liability, so the portfolio starts with no gain; the portfolio is contributed to the BV at that value, with no tax on the contribution.

Top marginal rates; the EUR 10,000 capital gains exemption, the EUR 859 dividend exemption and the 20% SME corporate rate on the first EUR 100,000 are ignored because the real family's income is about EUR 1 million a year.
The securities-account tax is taken at 0.30% on the whole portfolio every year, with the 10% cap ignored (it matters only up to about EUR 1.03 million). The tax is assumed not deductible in the BV.
The BV's running cost is the upper end of an accountant's quote (EUR 4,500) and excludes directors, investment management and audit.
No lifetime gifts are modelled; the engine has deaths only.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: gifts. A registered gift of movables to a child costs a flat 3% in Flanders and Brussels (against 27% at death above EUR 250,000), and an unregistered gift (bank transfer) is tax-free if the donor survives five years (Vlaamse Codex Fiscaliteit). The engine only models deaths, so the main Belgian planning tool is absent from the figures.

Needs an engine change: Flemish inheritance tax is calculated separately on the movable and on the immovable part of an estate, each from the bottom bracket (Flemish Tax Authority). The engine adds the EUR 5 million home to the portfolio and applies one scale, which slightly overstates the tax (the 3% and 9% bands apply twice by law).

A Belgian private foundation (private stichting) was considered and rejected: gifts to it cost 5.5% in Flanders (8.5% by bequest) and the assets leave the founder's estate, but since 2024 it pays an annual patrimony tax of 0.15% / 0.30% / 0.45% (the last above EUR 500,000, so about 0.45% of a EUR 30 million portfolio), is also liable for the securities-account tax and the 2026 capital gains tax, and the founder may not receive benefits from it, so it cannot fund the parents' EUR 400,000 a year. It is used for succession planning and asset protection, not as a portfolio vehicle. The tax on distributions to beneficiaries was not researched.
A foreign foundation or trust was rejected: the Cayman tax (art. 5/1 and 220/1 CIR 92) taxes the founder on the income of a foreign legal construction as if received directly (Circular 2024/C/79).

The payout from the BV is modelled at the flat 30% dividend withholding. A liquidation reserve released after a waiting period (9.8% after 3 years for reserves created after 30 December 2025) would lower it, but the engine has no timing for it.
The 0.30% securities-account rate rests on two bank notes (KBC, Bank van Breda) and Lexgo; the Programme Law text in the Moniteur belge was not opened, and PwC and Wikifin pages still show 0.15%.

Citations not opened or only partly read: art. 215, 192 and 22 CIR 92 and art. 269 section 1 (taken from the sources named, not read in the code); Flemish Codex Fiscaliteit article for the tariff (the Flemish Tax Authority page was used).
